readerTitle: 24 jams, 6 jams, and the trouble with famous studies
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Iyengar & Lepper 2000, 이후 메타분석) + 가상 사례 (찻잎 가게, 진열 위치 실험)
insight: 유명한 연구 결과는 내 사업의 법칙이 아니라 검증할 가설이다.
misconception: 선택지가 많으면 항상 덜 팔린다. 논문이나 블로그에 나온 효과는 내 사업에도 그대로 나타난다.

sources.text: Iyengar & Lepper (2000). When Choice Is Demotivating. J. of Personality and Social Psychology.
Scheibehenne, Greifeneder & Todd (2010). Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload. J. of Consumer Research.
Chernev, Böckenholt & Goodman (2015). Choice Overload: A Conceptual Review and Meta-Analysis. J. of Consumer Psychology.

factChecks.note: 원 연구 수치(24종 vs 6종, 멈춘 비율 60% vs 40%, 멈춘 사람 중 구매 3% vs 30%)는 Iyengar & Lepper(2000) 연구 1의 결과입니다.
Scheibehenne 외(2010) 메타분석은 50개 실험을 묶었고, 평균 효과 크기가 거의 0이었습니다. 효과가 아예 없다는 결론이 아니라 조건에 따라 달라진다는 결론입니다. 카드에도 그렇게 썼습니다.
Chernev 외(2015)가 제시한 조건(선택지의 복잡성, 결정 과제의 어려움, 선호의 불확실성, 결정 목표)을 쉬운 말로 풀었습니다. 표현을 단순하게 하면서 조건 목록을 줄였습니다.
CUS-05-04 "Choice overload" 레슨과 겹치지 않도록, 이 레슨은 선택 과부하 자체보다 연구 결과를 해석하는 법에 초점을 둡니다.

cards.title: 24 jams, 6 jams, and the trouble with famous studies
body: You've probably heard it: give people too many choices and they buy less. The proof is usually a study about jam.
The study was real. The rule people took from it is shakier.

image.label: A long table of jam jars, one shopper walking away
image.brief: 시식 테이블에 잼 병 24개가 빼곡히 놓여 있고, 쇼핑객 한 명이 빈손으로 지나가는 장면. 3D 클레이 스타일, 따뜻한 색감.

cards.title: A consultant wants you to cut your range.
body: You run a tea shop that stocks 60 teas. A consultant cites the jam study and tells you to cut down to 10.

options.text: Cut to 10. The research is clear
options.feedback: The research is less clear than it sounds, as you'll see. And cutting 50 products is hard to undo if you're wrong.

options.text: Keep the range, add a 'start here' shelf of 6, and test both
options.feedback: This tests the idea in your own shop. If simplifying helps, you'll see it. If it doesn't, you've lost little.

options.text: Add more teas. More choice, more sales
options.feedback: Possibly, but that's also a guess. And every product you add brings its own inventory costs.

cards.title: 24 jams vs 6 jams
body: In 2000, Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting table in a California grocery store. Some days it had 24 jams, other days 6.

groups.label: Shoppers who stopped at the table

cards.callout: More choice drew more people in, but far fewer of them bought. It became one of the most quoted findings in business.

cards.title: Other researchers struggled to find the same effect.
body: In 2010, Benjamin Scheibehenne and colleagues combined 50 experiments on choice overload. On average, the effect was close to **zero**.
Some studies found more choice hurt sales. Others found it helped. Many found little difference.
A 2015 review found choice overload does appear, but only under certain conditions.

cards.title: When famous findings don't replicate
body: A finding **replicates** when other researchers repeat the study and get a similar result. Many famous results in psychology and marketing replicate weakly, or only under narrow conditions.
Common reasons: small samples, one specific setting, and the fact that surprising results get published and shared more than unsurprising ones.

image.label: One bold result, many faint repeats
image.brief: 큰 굵은 막대 하나(원 연구) 옆에 작고 흐린 막대 여러 개(재현 실험). 일부는 위로, 일부는 아래로 향함.

cards.title: Choice overload depends on the situation.
list: **The options are hard to compare.** Many features, no clear differences.
**People don't know what they want yet.**
cards.callout: A shopper who already knows they want Earl Grey isn't overwhelmed by 60 teas.

cards.title: Don't swing to the opposite rule.
body: Weak replication doesn't prove the original idea false. It shows the idea is **conditional**. Too many confusing options can still hurt.
The mistake is treating any single study, or any "psychology hack", as a law for your business.
cards.softwareNote: Online, the same habit looks like copying another company's A/B test, such as a button color that "lifted sales 21%". Run it on your own traffic before you change anything.

cards.title: A trade magazine says eye-level shelves lift sales 30%.
body: It cites one retailer's results. Your store manager wants to rearrange every shelf this weekend. What do you do?

options.feedback: One retailer, one report, unknown conditions. A big number from someone else's store is a reason to test, not to act.

options.text: Try it in a few aisles first and compare
options.feedback: Cheap, reversible, and it tells you about your customers, not theirs.

options.text: Ignore it. Shelf position never matters
options.feedback: The effect may be smaller than claimed, but "never" is also an untested rule. If a test is cheap, run it.

cards.title: A famous study is a hypothesis for your business, not a rule.
body: Before using a research finding, ask three questions: How big was the study? Has anyone repeated it? Do its conditions match yours?
**Try it today:** think of one rule you follow because you read it somewhere. How could you test it in your own business?
